newsitem.title: Austria: Austria ends Creditanstalt battle with a bang. [CORRECTED 23:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Austria ends Creditanstalt battle with a bang. [CORRECTED 23:30 GMT]

text.p: Austria ended Europe's longest privatisation battle in the small hours of Sunday by selling flagship bank Creditanstalt to former arch-rival Bank Austria, heralding a shakeup of the country's coveted banking system.

After an 11-hour crisis meeting of coalition leaders the feuding partners hammered out a deal that let both sides save face and which they said was in the best interest of both the Austrian taxpayer and the country's financial system.

"The sale was successful, especially for the interests of the Austrian taxpayer and for shareholders of Creditanstalt. We managed to get the best possible price," Finance Minister Viktor Klima told a news conference just hours after closing the book on the seven-year selloff project.

The sale of Creditanstalt, one-time banker to the Habsburg family of Austro-Hungarian emperors, divided the coalition of dominant Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party and pushed the government to the brink of collapse.

The conservatives lost their main battle -- to save blue-blooded Creditanstalt from being sold to Bank Austria, which is controlled by the Social Democrat-led City of Vienna -- but scored on a range of side issues that are likely to make the deal more expensive for Bank Austria than projected.
Creditanstalt, established in 1855 to finance the development of the Austrian empire's railway network, will retain its independence for the next five years.

Over the next seven years (corrects from five years), Bank Austria will gradually be taken out of public control. Full privatisation of Austria's top bank was the main stumbling block in the negotiations.
Another conservative demand was to ensure that Creditanstalt's small shareholders receive a competitive price.

Klima said Bank Austria would offer small shareholders an extra two schillings per ordinary share to buy the 30 percent of voting shares not yet owned by the state -- a paltry premium of 0.3 percent over their market price.

According to the coalition agreement, the state's 19 percent stake in Bank Austria would be floated immediately, while the 45 percent stake held by the City of Vienna's Anteilsverwaltung Zentralsparkasse (AVZ) foundation would be cut to below 20 percent within seven years.

AVZ guarantees Bank Austria's liabilities, ensuring it a AAA rating, but the conservatives want AVZ's financial responsibility removed fully, which would likely cost Bank Austria its top-rating and an extra 100 million schillings per year to finance its debt.

A group of international financial and industrial interests led by Austro-Italian insurer EA-Generali made little effort on Sunday to hide its dismay at having been outbid by Bank Austria, whose offer topped that of the group by almost three billion schillings.
"We regret the decision...We submitted the most attractive offer for the long-term good of Austria's economy," EA-Generali chief Dietrich Karner said in a tightly-worded statement.
The mood inside Creditanstalt's historic central Vienna headquarters was hardly better. A spokesman for the bank told Reuters it had not even been informed about its new owners.

The link-up of Austria's two top banks will create a financial powerhouse with some 1,400 billion schillings ($126 billion) in total assets, holding wide-ranging stakes in many of the country's blue-chip companies.
Together, the two banks wield almost total control over Austria's overcrowded retail banking sector, raising the likelihood of a large number of branch closures and job cuts. ($1=11.09 Schilling)
